title: Cursor, which got its start with Kimi K2.5, tells Congress: intends to gradually phase out Chinese large models
excerpt: In Cursor's rise, Chinese open-source large models played a prominent role. Now, however, the company has voluntarily submitted a “farewell plan” to the U.S. Co
content_html:
In Cursor's rise, Chinese open-source large models played a prominent role. Now, however, the company has voluntarily submitted a “farewell plan” to the U.S. Congress. According to U.S. media reports, Anysphere, the developer of Cursor, reported to Congress that it intends to study gradually abandoning open-source AI large models from Chinese companies, though there is not yet a clear timetable for a complete shutdown.

The timing is especially intriguing. U.S. officials have recently been investigating American companies' use of Chinese open-source large models, and Cursor is now stepping forward to signal that it will cater to Congress's demands. It is hard to ignore one basic fact: the company's current business is propped up precisely by Chinese large models. Cursor's most important advance this year was building its own Composer2 large model on top of Moonshot AI's Kimi K2.5 foundation model. After the product launched, it was widely praised, and its user base surged.

Even though Composer2 incorporates Cursor's own technology and data, if you remove the foundation layer provided by Chinese large models, the cost of developing its own model would be real money and time: it would have to spend large sums on training and waste a great deal of time. In other words, Kimi K2.5's key role in boosting Cursor's business is an obvious part of the equation in this business. While reaping the dividends of Chinese open-source AI, it is signaling under official pressure that it will phase out Chinese AI—the irony is unmistakable.

The phase-out process will not be quick, but Cursor may have already paved its way out. xAI, owned by Musk, just acquired Cursor this year for $60 billion. In the future, its foundation model will sooner or later shift to the Grok series—even if Grok's coding ability is not particularly outstanding right now, that shift is only a matter of time.
